docs.text:
Question Proposed answer Evidence location Induction Doxycycline induces OsTIR1; IAA 500 μM activates the AID pathway; asunaprevir 3 μM inhibits SMASh cleavage. For immunoblotting, doxycycline is 1 μg/ml for 2 h before IAA/Asv. Together these are called DIA. Fig. 1A, F; “Immunoblotting” methods. Measurement Whole-cell immunoblots, ImageJ quantification and GAPDH normalisation, compared with control protein levels; three experiments for Fig. 1D–E. Fig. 1D–E; “Immunoblotting”. Efficiency Quantified: authors report approximately 50% depleted within 1 h and less than 5% remaining within 2–4 h. Do not invent separate exact endpoints from blot appearance. First Results subsection; Fig. 1D–E. Kinetics Time course above; combined activation is more effective than either system alone. This is not a fitted intrinsic half-life. Fig. 1D–F. Basal depletion Not reported in the inspected evidence as a dedicated basal-degradation measurement; provisional pending Appendix review. Untreated controls do not prove no leakiness. Main Results and Fig. 1–2. Recovery Not reported in the inspected evidence; provisional pending Appendix review. EdU washout is not DIA washout or cyclin recovery. “EdU pulse chase” methods; Fig. 5A–C.

Keep protocol differences visible: widefield live-cell microscopy specifies 2 μg/ml doxycycline; Fig. 4A specifies 3 h before IAA/Asv addition. Do not apply the immunoblot protocol to every experiment.

docs.title: Function after depletion and specificity
docs.text: Protein/background Outcome and controls Evidence location A2dd Depletion reduces mitotic entry, increases the 4N population and prevents colony formation. G2-specific tracking supports a requirement for A2 in mitotic entry, not just an earlier replication defect. Fig. 2B–E; Fig. 4A–C. B1dd B1 depletion reduces but does not prevent colony formation; no discernible cell-cycle phase-distribution change is reported. Fig. 2B–D. B1dd/B2ko Depleting B1 when B2 is absent permits mitotic entry but causes segregation/cytokinesis failure and prevents proliferation. Fig. 2B–E; Fig. 3A–D. A2 specificity Reciprocal cyclin-abundance checks and siRNA provide support. Wee1/B55 interventions bypass the block; they are not same-protein A2 rescue. No degradation-resistant A2 rescue was identified in the inspected sources. Fig. 1G; Fig. 2H–K; Fig. 4–5. B1 specificity Cyclin B1–YFP and B1–YFP–NLS rescue segregation/cytokinesis defects; YFP alone does not. This supports the causal role of B-type cyclin loss and functionality of the rescue proteins. EV4A–C and accompanying Results.

docs.title: Function: mixed, not simply normal
docs.text:
Proposed form answer: mixed. Binding affinity is retained, but signalling and morphine responses are reduced. “Impaired” is also defensible if the explanation includes the preserved readouts. “Retained in assays tested” without qualification is not supported.

The following values are printed in the table above Supplementary Fig. 2 (p. 7), not estimated from curves. They are mean ± SEM, n = 5 per group.

Assay WT HA-MOP KI/KI Conclusion DAMGO binding affinity, Kd 1.91 ± 0.23 nM 2.04 ± 0.41 nM No significant affinity change reported. Binding capacity, Bmax 46.5 ± 3.7 fmol/mg protein 20.3 ± 1.8 fmol/mg protein Fewer receptor binding sites, P < 0.01. DAMGO-stimulated GTPγS binding, EC50 175 ± 23 nM 369 ± 81 nM Reduced potency, P < 0.05. Maximum GTPγS response, % basal 153 ± 5 127 ± 3 Reduced response, P < 0.01. Basal is 100%; these are not percentage increases above baseline.

Further evidence:

  • Morphine response is reduced: hot-plate antinociception is lower than WT and resembles heterozygous MOP knockout controls. See Supplementary Fig. 2f and supplementary “Hot-plate test” methods.
  • Agonist-dependent phosphorylation is retained: high-efficacy agonists induce multisite phosphorylation. This supports retained regulation, not complete physiological equivalence. See main Fig. 3 and Table 1.
  • Body weight and basal pain responses are unchanged: these do not override the drug-response deficit. See Supplementary Fig. 2d–e.

Interpretation limit: reduced tissue signalling may reflect reduced receptor abundance. These assays do not isolate a signalling defect per receptor molecule.

Source-location trap: the main Results text points to S2b for Bmax. The supplement actually puts saturation binding/Bmax in S2a and the table, and GTPγS signalling in S2b.

docs.text: A small tag and unchanged binding affinity do not establish normal function. This is a useful detection model with measurable biological alterations—not a completely nonfunctional receptor, but not an unqualified substitute for WT either.

docs.title: Two agents, two different questions
docs.text:
You want to know whether anyone has tagged your phosphatase, where the tag went and whether the tagged protein still worked. A broad search can return hundreds or thousands of papers, most of which will not answer that question.

Agent Task What a useful evaluation checks 1: abstract screening Recognise tagging information and recommend papers to open Does it miss tagging studies, admit irrelevant ones or invent details absent from the abstract? 2: full-text extraction Recover the tag, method, terminus and functional evidence Are its claims supported by the full text, including methods and supplements?

The fifty supplied abstracts test the first task. They are not necessarily about your gene. The full-text task needs separate manual full-text annotations: an abstract answer cannot establish what a full paper says. See Evaluating agents for the shared principles.

docs.title: Evidence, not plausible guesses
docs.text:
Abstracts often name a tag without specifying its location or integration method. If the source does not state a field, record not_stated—even when you have a plausible guess. For the screening decision, use cannot_tell when there is not enough information to decide whether tagging occurred.

Two recurring traps are natural degron motifs, which are part of a protein's sequence, and small-molecule degraders, which can remove a protein without adding a tag. Neither alone establishes a tagging study. Conversely, GFP or an epitope tag can supply relevant tagging precedent even when no degradation experiment was done.

“CRISPR” does not establish an endogenous tag. Even “knock-in” needs a stated integration site before you can assign the tag to the protein's native locus. Try the examples.

docs.title: How human answers become a reference
docs.text:
You and your supervisor annotate independently. Keep both original records. Before inspecting model answers, review disagreements together and record a separate adjudicated answer with its reasoning. If a rule needs clarification, record the change and apply it consistently.

Agreement is useful evidence of consistency, not proof of correctness or an accuracy ceiling. Two people can share a mistaken interpretation. Disagreements may reveal an unclear rule, missing evidence or a simple error; all are worth examining without treating them as personal failures.

docs.title: What the model's score can tell you
docs.text:
The supplied set contains roughly ten tagging abstracts and forty others, including deliberately difficult negatives. That is a test set, not a promise about the composition of your gene's literature. Its accuracy does not automatically transfer to a new search.

Report Why Sensitivity and specificity Separate missed tagging studies from irrelevant papers admitted. Counts and uncertainty With roughly ten positives, one missed paper changes sensitivity substantially. Uncertain decisions Report cannot_tell separately; agree how it is handled before scoring. Per-field agreement and unsupported values A correct screening decision can still come with an invented locus or terminus.

An all-negative screener could achieve about 80% accuracy here while missing every tagging study. That is why overall accuracy alone is misleading.

docs.title: Then apply the workflow to your gene
docs.text:
Keep the query, search date, candidate list and agent decisions. Read the full texts of yes and cannot_tell candidates. Also manually audit a sample of rejected abstracts, chosen before reading their full texts, to look for false negatives. Agree the sample size at supervision and report its limits; this is a check, not proof that nothing was missed.

For Agent 2, first produce and lock independent manual full-text annotations on an agreed evaluation subset, without AI. Record unavailable papers rather than treating them as negative results. Keep source locations for evidence in methods, results and supplements. Confirm the recording workflow and deadline with your supervisor before starting; do not reuse or overwrite the frozen abstract records.

A surviving tagged cell is useful precedent, but it does not establish normal protein function. Ask what was actually tested—activity, localisation, complementation or something else—and whether the organism, cell model, tag and expression context are relevant to your design.

The final claim should be “we found this evidence within this search”, not “nobody has ever tagged it” simply because the agent returned no candidates.

docs.title: Abstract 1
docs.text:
Ran-GTP assembles a specialized spindle structure for accurate chromosome segregation in medaka early embryos. Nat Commun, 2024. PMID 38302485.

Despite drastic cellular changes during cleavage, a mitotic spindle assembles in each blastomere to accurately segregate duplicated chromosomes. Mechanisms of mitotic spindle assembly have been extensively studied using small somatic cells. However, mechanisms of spindle assembly in large vertebrate embryos remain little understood. Here, we establish functional assay systems in medaka (Oryzias latipes) embryos by combining CRISPR knock-in with auxin-inducible degron technology. Live imaging reveals several unexpected features of microtubule organization and centrosome positioning that achieve rapid, accurate cleavage. Importantly, Ran-GTP assembles a dense microtubule network at the metaphase spindle center that is essential for chromosome segregation in early embryos. This unique spindle structure is remodeled into a typical short, somatic-like spindle after blastula stages, when Ran-GTP becomes dispensable for chromosome segregation. We propose that despite the presence of centrosomes, the chromosome-derived Ran-GTP pathway has essential roles in functional spindle assembly in large, rapidly dividing vertebrate early embryos, similar to acentrosomal spindle assembly in oocytes.

Discuss: which experimental details can you record directly, and which would you need to investigate further?

docs.title: Abstract 2
docs.text:
One-step multiplex toolkit for efficient generation of conditional gene silencing human cell lines. Mol Biol Cell, 2021. PMID 33979199.

Loss-of-function analysis is one of the major arsenals we have for understanding gene functions in mammalian cells. For analysis of essential genes, the major challenge is to develop simple methodologies for tight and rapid inducible gene inactivation. One approach involves CRISPR-Cas9-mediated disruption of the endogenous locus in conjunction with the expression of a rescue construct, which can subsequently be turned off to produce a gene inactivation effect. Here we describe the development of a set of Sleeping Beauty transposon-based vectors for expressing auxin-inducible degron (AID)-tagged genes under the regulation of a tetracycline-controlled promoter. The dual transcriptional and degron-mediated post-translational regulation allows rapid and tight silencing of protein expression in mammalian cells. We demonstrated that both non-essential and essential genes could be targeted in human cell lines using a one-step transfection method. Moreover, multiple genes could be simultaneously or sequentially targeted, allowing inducible inactivation of multiple genes. These resources enable highly efficient generation of conditional gene silencing cell lines to facilitate functional studies of essential genes.

Discuss: sketch the experimental strategy. Which words support each part of your sketch?

docs.title: Abstract 3
docs.text:
EBF1 is continuously required for stabilizing local chromatin accessibility in pro-B cells. PNAS, 2022. PMID 36409886.

The establishment of de novo chromatin accessibility in lymphoid progenitors requires the "pioneering" function of transcription factor (TF) early B cell factor 1 (EBF1), which binds to naïve chromatin and induces accessibility by recruiting the BRG1 chromatin remodeler subunit. However, it remains unclear whether the function of EBF1 is continuously required for stabilizing local chromatin accessibility. To this end, we replaced EBF1 by EBF1-FKBP^F36V in pro-B cells, allowing the rapid degradation by adding the degradation TAG13 (dTAG13) dimerizer. EBF1 degradation results in a loss of genome-wide EBF1 occupancy and EBF1-targeted BRG1 binding. Chromatin accessibility was rapidly diminished at EBF1-binding sites with a preference for sites whose occupancy requires the pioneering activity of the C-terminal domain of EBF1. Diminished chromatin accessibility correlated with altered gene expression. Thus, continuous activity of EBF1 is required for the stable maintenance of the transcriptional and epigenetic state of pro-B cells.

Discuss: did your group interpret any phrase differently? What evidence would settle the disagreement?

docs.title: Abstract 4
docs.text:
Two diphosphorylated degrons control c-Myc degradation by the Fbw7 tumor suppressor. Sci Adv, 2022. PMID 35089787.

c-Myc (hereafter, Myc) is a cancer driver whose abundance is regulated by the SCF^Fbw7 ubiquitin ligase and proteasomal degradation. Fbw7 binds to a phosphorylated Myc degron centered at threonine 58 (T58), and mutations of Fbw7 or T58 impair Myc degradation in cancers. Here, we identify a second Fbw7 phosphodegron at Myc T244 that is required for Myc ubiquitylation and acts in concert with T58 to engage Fbw7. While Ras-dependent Myc serine 62 phosphorylation (pS62) is thought to stabilize Myc by preventing Fbw7 binding, we find instead that pS62 greatly enhances Fbw7 binding and is an integral part of a high-affinity degron. Crystallographic studies revealed that both degrons bind Fbw7 in their diphosphorylated forms and that the T244 degron is recognized via a unique mode involving Fbw7 arginine 689 (R689), a mutational hotspot in cancers. These insights have important implications for Myc-associated tumorigenesis and therapeutic strategies targeting Myc stability.

Discuss: what is the relationship between the mechanism described and the screening question you are trying to answer?

docs.title: Abstract 5
docs.text:
Nuclear Magnetic Resonance-based fragment screen of the E3 ligase Fem-1 homolog B. Protein Sci, 2025. PMID 41229306.

Targeted protein degradation using PROTACs (PROteolysis TArgeting Chimeras) has emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy, largely relying on a small number of E3 ubiquitin ligases such as CRBN and VHL. However, resistance, toxicity, and poor oral bioavailability limit the utility of PROTACs and highlight the need to expand the E3 ligase toolbox. Fem-1 homolog B (FEM1B) is a lesser-known E3 ligase that offers a promising alternative due to its broad expression and ability to recognize diverse degron motifs. Here, we describe the development of a stable construct of FEM1B, the results of a protein-observed NMR-based fragment screen using this construct, and the X-ray structures of some of the fragment hits when bound to the protein. From these results, new PROTACs utilizing FEM1B as the E3 ligase may be discovered, providing an alternative E3 ligase for targeted protein degradation.

Discuss: what does the abstract tell you about the experimental construct? What, if anything, remains unresolved for your screening decision?

docs.text:
A terminus choice with the evidence behind it — precedent, modifications, isoforms A guide RNA with your reasoning about cut site and off-targets Homology arms the right length, ending exactly where they must A donor cassette, linkers and arms, assembled in frame

Prepare the human design in SnapGene and be able to defend each choice. Keep it independent of the cloning agent's proposed design. Preserve the version you present on 8 December before inspecting agent-generated designs.

docs.title: Then compare with the cloning agent
docs.text:
After the presentations on 8 December, your supervisor demonstrates the cloning agent with and without DNAgent. During the following week, run the comparison and use the agent to help work out how to quantify human–agent differences. Record the comparison criteria, checks and any changes to them; do not overwrite your original human design.

Bring the results so far and unresolved questions to the 15 December summary and review.

docs.title: What you are given
docs.text:
The modification, isoform and structure data for your protein. Mapping all of that is a database job rather than a judgement one, and it would eat the rest of your term.

Interpreting it is the work. A tag that blocks a phosphorylation site, or lands on a terminus that only one of three isoforms shares, is a tag that will waste a year at the bench.

docs.title: Name the trap in advance
docs.text:
The frame. The arm has to end exactly on a codon boundary, because the linker is fixed and will not absorb a slip.

An off-by-one here produces a construct that looks perfectly right on a map and translates into nonsense. It is the most common single error in this kind of design, and nothing about the sequence announces it — you only find it by translating and reading the protein.

docs.title: How this connects back
docs.text:
Your literature work told you whether anyone has done this before, at which terminus, and whether the protein still worked. This is where that becomes a decision.

If precedent exists, say why you are following or departing from it. If it does not, say what you are inferring from and how confident you are. A design with honest uncertainty stated is worth more than a confident one that hides its assumptions.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You have a guide, arms and a donor that assemble in frame.
  • You can say why that terminus and not the other one.
  • Someone can ask "what if the paper you based this on used an overexpression construct?" and you have an answer.
  • Your human design is preserved before comparison with the cloning agent.

docs.title: Phase 3 · Analysis and write-up
docs.text:
Literature evaluations · 17–24 November

Assemble and lock the human references on 17 November, then run the evaluations and analyse the results for 24 November. Cloning-agent comparisons follow the human design presentations on 8 December, with summary and review on 15 December. See the project schedule.

From mid-November to the end of term, then the vacation at your own pace.

Score the model runs against your annotations, work out what the numbers mean, and write the thesis.

docs.title: What you are given
docs.text: Your locked answers from phases 1 and 2 The agent runs the same questions, answered twice — once by a bare agent, once by the same agent equipped with the tools built for the job Everyone's answers on the shared protein the five of you against each other

docs.title: The number that makes the rest readable
docs.text: The five sets of answers on the shared protein give inter-rater agreement — how much careful people disagree with each other on the same material. This is context for interpreting model scores, not an accuracy ceiling. People can share errors, and an agent can sometimes be right when a reader is wrong. Keep independent records, investigate disagreements and distinguish agreement with the reference from scientific correctness.

docs.title: Agent access and independent work
docs.text:
Accounts are issued on 10 November, with a hands-on session. Use the agent for analysis, code and later writing, but not for the three independent full-text reference papers prepared during 10–17 November. Reference answers must be locked before model output is inspected.

After the 8 December cloning-agent demonstration, use the agent to help develop a way to quantify human–agent cloning differences. Preserve the human design first, document the comparison criteria and retain the raw results.

Keep a log of what you asked and what you had to fix. It goes in as an appendix. See Your Claude account.

docs.title: Over the vacation
docs.text: Use the 15 December review to agree remaining analysis and a writing plan. Finish the protein introduction after Christmas; its exact deadline will be confirmed.

docs.title: Circadian clock and breast cancer
docs.text:
Does the circadian clock matter in breast cancer, and what can public data add? This project answers it with the literature first, then with tumour data (TCGA, DepMap), working with an AI agent throughout and documenting how.

It uses the same tools and rules as the rest of FYP26, applied to a different question. Where a shared page already covers something, this section links to it.

docs.title: Phase 1 · Literature
docs.text:
Find the papers that matter in a large literature, and measure how well a classifier does that job before trusting it.

flowchart LR
    A["PubMed search<br/>circadian AND cancer<br/>~7,200 abstracts"] --> B["Classifier (Jev)<br/>seven questions"]
    B --> C["Papers taken forward<br/>(question 7)<br/>read in full"]
    D["Your answers on<br/>300 sample abstracts<br/>no AI"] --> E["How good is the<br/>classifier compared<br/>with a human?"]
    B --> E
Part Task Output 1 · Abstract classification Classify 300 abstracts by hand Your locked answers 2 · Evaluation Compare the classifier with your answers; check what the PubMed search misses Agreement per question, and the errors behind it 3 · Full scan Run the classifier on all ~7,200 abstracts and pick papers to read in full A ranked reading list

Parts 2 and 3 get their own pages when you reach them.

docs.title: Why two checks
docs.text:
The literature passes through two filters, and each can lose papers:

  • The PubMed query decides which abstracts the classifier ever sees. A paper it misses is gone for good, so it is deliberately broad.
  • The classifier sorts what is left. Your answers measure how well.

This is the same logic as the main project's evaluation: Why evaluate first? and Evaluating agents.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Getting ready to use the agents: VS Code, uv and Claude Code.
  • Ground rules for the agent and Your Claude account: why your answers are made without AI.
  • What an AI agent is.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Classify 300 abstracts against seven questions, by hand, to create an independent reference. The classifier (Jev) then answers the same questions for the same abstracts, and you measure how good it is compared with a human. Why this evaluation matters.

docs.title: Time
docs.text: About ten hours: two minutes an abstract once you are practised. Spread it over several sittings; label quality drops after an hour. Your supervisor sets the deadline.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Get CB1_items.json from your supervisor. It holds 300 shuffled abstracts: some about the circadian clock in breast cancer, some about other cancers, some about neither.
  • Classify the twelve examples and compare with their solutions.
  • Keep AI out of this task, and do not open the full papers until your answers are locked.

docs.title: The seven questions
docs.text:
The same questions, with the same wording, go to you and to the classifier.

# Question Options 1 Circadian: the abstract reports research on the circadian clock, circadian rhythms or circadian disruption (for example shift work or light at night) yes, no, unsure 2 Cancer: the abstract reports research on cancer or tumours yes, no, unsure 3 Breast cancer: the abstract reports research on breast cancer specifically yes, no, unsure 4 Clock gene: the abstract reports results on at least one named core clock gene or protein: BMAL1 (ARNTL), CLOCK, PER1–3, CRY1–2, NR1D1–2 (REV-ERB) yes, no, unsure 5 Evidence: the main kind of evidence reported patient_samples_or_cohort, cell_lines, animal_model, epidemiology, review, not_stated 6 Expression data: the abstract reports gene or protein expression measured in human tumour or patient samples yes, no, unsure 7 Full text: take the paper forward. The abstract reports original results that link at least one named core clock gene or protein to cancer: tumour growth or cancer cell behaviour, expression in tumours, patient outcome, or treatment response yes, no, unsure
  • Answer all seven for every abstract, including the ones that are not about the clock or cancer. A clear no is as useful to the evaluation as a yes.
  • unsure: the abstract does not settle it. Do not guess from what would make biological sense.
  • Full text: yes and unsure both queue the paper for full-text reading. Reviews and commentaries are no, and so is shift-work epidemiology that names no clock gene. Any cancer counts, not only breast.
  • epidemiology: population studies, such as shift work and cancer risk. If several kinds of evidence apply, choose the one the conclusions rest on.
  • The trap: "clock" in another sense. An epigenetic clock or mitotic clock is not the circadian clock. Melatonin counts as circadian only when the abstract frames it as a rhythm or clock signal.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the circadian annotation tool and load CB1_items.json.
  2. Read the title and abstract.
  3. Answer the seven questions.
  4. Export after every sitting. Keep the downloaded JSON: browser storage is not a backup.
  5. Check that the tool reports 300/300 complete, then send the final export to your supervisor.

docs.title: Resume from a saved export
docs.text:
In the same browser, load CB1_items.json again to resume browser-saved work. On another browser, or after clearing storage:

  1. Load CB1_items.json.
  2. Click Restore saved annotations and choose your latest export.
  3. Check the record count, then confirm.

Restore replaces current answers rather than merging them. Export current work first if you need to keep it.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• All 300 items have all seven answers.
  • The export reports 300/300 complete.
  • You have sent the final export and kept a local copy.
  • Your supervisor confirms it is locked before you see any classifier answers.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text: Your supervisor runs the classifier on the same 300 abstracts. You then compare its answers with yours, question by question: where does it agree, where does it miss papers, where does it include papers it should not? Question 7 matters most: it decides which papers are read in full. You will also test whether asking it directly beats combining the simpler questions (cancer, clock gene, not a review). That comparison, and checking how many relevant papers the PubMed search itself misses, is Part 2.

docs.title: If you get stuck
docs.text: Use unsure when the abstract does not settle a question, and not_stated for evidence. Ask your supervisor about a convention if you need to; do not look up the paper or ask AI to resolve an answer.

docs.title: Examples · Twelve abstracts with solutions
docs.text:
Classify these twelve before you start your 300, in the same tool you will use for the real set. They are real abstracts, separate from your set. The questions and rules are on the Part 1 page.

  1. Download CB0_items.json. Keep the file name exactly as it is.
  2. Open the annotation tool and load it. Practice answers are saved separately from your 300.
  3. Answer all seven questions for each abstract. Export when you finish.
  4. Compare your export with the solutions below. The abstracts are also printed here, in the same order (EX-01 is abstract 1).

docs.title: Abstract 1
docs.text:
Loss of circadian clock gene expression is associated with tumor progression in breast cancer. Cell Cycle, 2014. PMID 25485508.

Several studies suggest a link between circadian rhythm disturbances and tumorigenesis. However, the association between circadian clock genes and prognosis in breast cancer has not been systematically studied. Therefore, we examined the expression of 17 clock components in tumors from 766 node-negative breast cancer patients that were untreated in both neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. In addition, their association with metastasis-free survival (MFS) and correlation to clinicopathological parameters were investigated. Aiming to estimate functionality of the clockwork, we studied clock gene expression relationships by correlation analysis. Higher expression of several clock genes (e.g., CLOCK, PER1, PER2, PER3, CRY2, NPAS2 and RORC) was found to be associated with longer MFS in univariate Cox regression analyses (HR<1 and FDR-adjusted P < 0.05). Stratification according to molecular subtype revealed prognostic relevance for PER1, PER3, CRY2 and NFIL3 in the ER+/HER2- subgroup, CLOCK and NPAS2 in the ER-/HER2- subtype, and ARNTL2 in HER2+ breast cancer. In the multivariate Cox model, only PER3 (HR = 0.66; P = 0.016) and RORC (HR = 0.42; P = 0.003) were found to be associated with survival outcome independent of established clinicopathological parameters. Pairwise correlations between functionally-related clock genes (e.g., PER2-PER3 and CRY2-PER3) were stronger in ER+, HER2- and low-grade carcinomas; whereas, weaker correlation coefficients were observed in ER- and HER2+ tumors, high-grade tumors and tumors that progressed to metastatic disease. In conclusion, loss of clock genes is associated with worse prognosis in breast cancer. Coordinated co-expression of clock genes, indicative of a functional circadian clock, is maintained in ER+, HER2-, low grade and non-metastasizing tumors but is compromised in more aggressive carcinomas.

Solution Circadian Cancer Breast Clock gene Evidence Expression Full text yes yes yes yes patient_samples_or_cohort yes yes

The clear case, and the kind of paper the project is looking for. Clock gene expression ("CLOCK, PER1, PER2, PER3, CRY2") is measured "in tumors from 766 node-negative breast cancer patients" and linked to metastasis-free survival. Every question is settled by the abstract.

docs.title: Abstract 2
docs.text:
Circadian Clock Gene bmal1 Acts as a Tumor Suppressor Gene in a Mice Model of Human Glioblastoma. Mol Neurobiol, 2024. PMID 38180613.

Glioblastomas derived from malignant astrocytes are the most common primary tumors of the central nervous system in humans, exhibiting very bad prognosis. Treatment with surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy (mainly using temozolomide), generates as much one-year survival. The circadian clock controls different aspects of tumor development, and its role in GBM is beginning to be explored. Here, the role of the canonic circadian clock gene bmal1 was studied in vivo in a nude mice model bearing human GBMs from LN229 cells xenografted orthotopically in the dorsal striatum. For that aim, a bmal1 knock-down was generated in LN229 cells by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing tool, and tumor progression was followed in male mice by measuring survival, tumor growth, cell proliferation and prognosis with CD44 marker, as well as astrocyte activation in the tumor microenvironment with GFAP and nestin markers. Disruption of bmal1 in the tumor decreased survival, increased tumor growth and CD44 expression, worsened motor performance, as well as increased GFAP expression in astrocytes at tumor microenvironment. In addition, survival and tumor progression was not affected in mice bearing LN229 wild type GBM that underwent circadian disruption by constant light, as compared to mice synchronized to 12:12 light-dark cycles. These results consistently demonstrate in an in vivo orthotopic model of human GBM, that bmal1 has a key role as a tumor suppressor gene regulating GBM progression.

Solution Circadian Cancer Breast Clock gene Evidence Expression Full text yes yes no yes animal_model no yes
  • Full text: yes. Original results link BMAL1 to tumour growth. Any cancer counts, not only breast; question 3 is there to filter later.
  • Evidence: animal_model. The knockdown is made in a cell line, but the conclusions rest on the mice ("in an in vivo orthotopic model").
  • Expression: no. CD44 and GFAP are measured in xenografts grown in mice. Human cells in a mouse are not human tumour or patient samples.

docs.title: Abstract 3
docs.text:
Rotating Night-Shift Work and the Risk of Breast Cancer in the Nurses' Health Studies. Am J Epidemiol, 2017. PMID 28541391.

In 2007, the International Agency for Research on Cancer declared shift work that involved circadian disruption to be a "probable" carcinogen (group 2A), noting that human evidence was limited. Using data from 2 prospective cohort studies, the Nurses' Health Study (1988-2012; n = 78,516) and Nurses' Health Study II (1989-2013; n = 114,559), we examined associations between rotating night-shift work and breast cancer risk. In the 2 cohorts, there were a total of 9,541 incident invasive breast malignancies and 24 years of follow-up. In the Nurses' Health Study, women with 30 years or more of shift work did not have a higher risk of breast cancer (hazard ratio (HR) = 0.95, 95% confidence interval (95% CI): 0.77, 1.17; P for trend = 0.63) compared with those who never did shift work, although follow-up occurred primarily after retirement from shift work. Among participants in the Nurses' Health Study II, who were younger than participants in the other cohort, the risk of breast cancer was significantly higher in women with 20 years or more of shift work at baseline, reflecting young-adult exposure (HR = 2.15, 95% CI: 1.23, 3.73; P for trend = 0.23), and was marginally significantly higher for women with 20 years or more of cumulative shift work when we used updated exposure information (HR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.00, 1.97; P for trend = 0.74). In conclusion, long-term rotating night-shift work was associated with a higher risk of breast cancer, particularly among women who performed shift work during young adulthood. Further studies should explore the role of shift work timing on breast cancer risk.

Solution Circadian Cancer Breast Clock gene Evidence Expression Full text yes yes yes no epidemiology no no
  • Circadian: yes. The abstract frames shift work as "circadian disruption".
  • Evidence: epidemiology. It is a population study of cancer risk. Two large cohorts are not patient samples: nothing is measured in tissue.
  • Full text: no. No clock gene is named, so it cannot feed the clock-gene evidence extraction, however relevant it is to the background of your thesis. Keep a note of papers like this for your introduction.

docs.title: Abstract 4
docs.text:
Susceptibility to hormone-mediated cancer is reflected by different tick rates of the epithelial and general epigenetic clock. Genome Biol, 2022. PMID 35189945.

BACKGROUND: A variety of epigenetic clocks utilizing DNA methylation changes have been developed; these clocks are either tissue-independent or designed to predict chronological age based on blood or saliva samples. Whether discordant tick rates between tissue-specific and general epigenetic clocks play a role in health and disease has not yet been explored.

RESULTS: Here we analyze 1941 cervical cytology samples, which contain a mixture of hormone-sensitive cervical epithelial cells and immune cells, and develop the WID general clock (Women's IDentification of risk), an epigenetic clock that is shared by epithelial and immune cells and optimized for cervical samples. We then develop the WID epithelial clock and WID immune clock, which define epithelial- and immune-specific clocks, respectively. We find that the WID-relative-epithelial-age (WID-REA), defined as the difference between the epithelial and general clocks, is significantly reduced in cervical samples from pre-menopausal women with breast cancer (OR 2.7, 95% CI 1.28-5.72). We find the same effect in normal breast tissue samples from pre-menopausal women at high risk of breast cancer and show that potential risk reducing anti-progesterone drugs can reverse this. In post-menopausal women, this directionality is reversed. Hormone replacement therapy consistently leads to a significantly lower WID-REA in cancer-free women, but not in post-menopausal women with breast or ovarian cancer.

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings imply that there are multiple epigenetic clocks, many of which are tissue-specific, and that the differential tick rate between these clocks may be an informative surrogate measure of disease risk.

Solution Circadian Cancer Breast Clock gene Evidence Expression Full text no yes yes no patient_samples_or_cohort no no
  • The trap. "Clock" appears eleven times, and none of them is the circadian clock. An epigenetic clock estimates age from DNA methylation. This is exactly the abstract a keyword search lets through and a careful reader screens out; it is a good test of the classifier too.
  • Expression: no. DNA methylation is not gene or protein expression.
  • Evidence: patient_samples_or_cohort. The results come from measurements on cervical and breast samples.

docs.title: Abstract 5
docs.text:
Induction of the CLOCK gene by E2-ERα signaling promotes the proliferation of breast cancer cells. PLoS One, 2014. PMID 24789043.

Growing genetic and epidemiological evidence suggests a direct connection between the disruption of circadian rhythm and breast cancer. Moreover, the expression of several molecular components constituting the circadian clock machinery has been found to be modulated by estrogen-estrogen receptor α (E2-ERα) signaling in ERα-positive breast cancer cells. In this study, we investigated the regulation of CLOCK expression by ERα and its roles in cell proliferation. Immunohistochemical analysis of human breast tumor samples revealed high expression of CLOCK in ERα-positive breast tumor samples. Subsequent experiments using ERα-positive human breast cancer cell lines showed that both protein and mRNA levels of CLOCK were up-regulated by E2 and ERα. In these cells, E2 promoted the binding of ERα to the EREs (estrogen-response elements) of CLOCK promoter, thereby up-regulating the transcription of CLOCK. Knockdown of CLOCK attenuated cell proliferation in ERα-positive breast cancer cells. Taken together, these results demonstrated that CLOCK could be an important gene that mediates cell proliferation in breast cancer cells.

Solution Circadian Cancer Breast Clock gene Evidence Expression Full text yes yes yes yes cell_lines yes yes
  • Evidence: cell_lines. One staining of tumour samples, then the conclusions rest on "ERα-positive human breast cancer cell lines".
  • Expression: yes. That one staining counts: CLOCK measured by immunohistochemistry "of human breast tumor samples". Questions 5 and 6 are independent; a cell-line paper can still say yes to 6.

docs.title: Abstract 6
docs.text:
Circadian rhythms and breast cancer: from molecular level to therapeutic advancements. J Cancer Res Clin Oncol, 2024. PMID 39266868.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Circadian rhythms, the endogenous biological clocks that govern physiological processes, have emerged as pivotal regulators in the development and progression of breast cancer. This comprehensive review delves into the intricate interplay between circadian disruption and breast tumorigenesis from multifaceted perspectives, encompassing biological rhythms, circadian gene regulation, tumor microenvironment dynamics, and genetic polymorphisms.

METHODS AND RESULTS: Epidemiological evidence underscores the profound impact of external factors, such as night shift work, jet lag, dietary patterns, and exercise routines, on breast cancer risk and progression through the perturbation of circadian homeostasis. The review elucidates the distinct roles of key circadian genes, including CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, and CRY, in breast cancer biology, highlighting their therapeutic potential as molecular targets. Additionally, it investigates how circadian rhythm dysregulation shapes the tumor microenvironment, fostering epithelial-mesenchymal transition, chronic inflammation, and immunosuppression, thereby promoting tumor progression and metastasis. Furthermore, the review sheds light on the association between circadian gene polymorphisms and breast cancer susceptibility, paving the way for personalized risk assessment and tailored treatment strategies.

CONCLUSIONS: Importantly, it explores innovative therapeutic modalities that harness circadian rhythms, including chronotherapy, melatonin administration, and traditional Chinese medicine interventions. Overall, this comprehensive review emphasizes the critical role of circadian rhythms in the pathogenesis of breast cancer and highlights the promising prospects for the development of circadian rhythm-based interventions to enhance treatment efficacy and improve patient outcomes.

Solution Circadian Cancer Breast Clock gene Evidence Expression Full text yes yes yes yes review no no
  • Evidence: review. "This comprehensive review". The heading "Methods and results" does not make it original research.
  • Clock gene: yes. CLOCK, BMAL1, PER and CRY are named. Question 4 only asks whether core clock genes are named and discussed; question 7 is where reviews are excluded.
  • Full text: no. Reviews are always no. Useful for your introduction, not for evidence extraction.

docs.title: Abstract 7
docs.text:
First-morning urinary melatonin and breast cancer risk in the Guernsey Study. Am J Epidemiol, 2014. PMID 24418683.

It has been hypothesized that suppressed nocturnal melatonin production is associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, but results from several small prospective studies of the association have been inconclusive. We examined the association between nocturnal melatonin and breast cancer risk in a case-control study nested within the Guernsey III Study, a British prospective cohort study (1977-2009). Concentrations of 6-sulfatoxymelatonin were measured in prediagnostic first-morning urine samples from 251 breast cancer cases and 727 matched controls. Conditional logistic regression models were used to calculate odds ratios for breast cancer in relation to 6-sulfatoxymelatonin level. No significant association was found between 6-sulfatoxymelatonin level and breast cancer risk, either overall (for highest third vs. lowest, multivariable-adjusted odds ratio = 0.90, 95% confidence interval: 0.61, 1.33) or by menopausal status. However, in a meta-analysis of all published prospective data, including 1,113 cases from 5 studies, higher 6-sulfatoxymelatonin levels were associated with lower breast cancer risk (for highest fourth vs. lowest, odds ratio = 0.81, 95% confidence interval: 0.66, 0.99). In summary, we found no evidence that 6-sulfatoxymelatonin level in a first-morning urine sample was associated with breast cancer risk among British women. However, overall the published data suggest a modest inverse association between melatonin levels and breast cancer risk. Further data are needed to confirm this association.

Solution Circadian Cancer Breast Clock gene Evidence Expression Full text no yes yes no epidemiology no no
  • Circadian: no. Melatonin is treated as a hormone level, never as a rhythm or clock signal. You may know the light-at-night hypothesis behind it; the abstract does not say it, so it does not count.
  • Evidence: epidemiology. A case-control study of cancer risk, plus a meta-analysis. Urine is measured, but the question is who gets cancer.

docs.title: Abstract 8
docs.text:
ARNTL2 is a Prognostic Biomarker and Correlates with Immune Cell Infiltration in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer. Pharmgenomics Pers Med, 2021. PMID 34785930.

BACKGROUND: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive breast cancer subtype and is associated with poor prognosis. The aberrant expression of circadian genes contributes to the origin and progression of breast cancer. The present study was designed to explore the potential function and prognosis value of circadian genes in TNBC.

METHODS: The transcriptome data of circadian genes were downloaded from The Cancer Genomic Atlas (TCGA), GSE25066 and GSE31448 datasets. The differential expressed circadian genes between non-TNBC and TNBC patients were analysed by Wilcoxon test. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses were employed to identify the prognostic circadian genes. Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) were performed to study the biological functions of ARNTL2. The composition of 22 immune cells in the tumour samples was estimated with CIBERSORT algorithm. The correlations between ARNTL2 expression and tumour-infiltrating immune cells were evaluated by Spearman correlation coefficient.

RESULTS: A total of 8 circadian genes were found to be differentially expressed between non-TNBC and TNBC, but only ARNTL2 has prognostic value. Multivariate Cox analysis identified that ARNTL2 was an independent prognosis factor for overall survival and relapse-free survival in TNBC patients. Functionally, ARNTL2 was mainly involved in immune response processes such as positive regulation of cytokine production, regulation of innate immune response, and cellular responses to molecules of bacterial origin. High expression of ARNTL2 was positively correlated with activated CD4 memory T cells, activated mast cells, and neutrophil infiltration and the expression of markers of neutrophils (ITGAM), dendritic cells (HLA-DRA, HLA-DPA1, ITGAM), Th1 (IL1B, STAT1), Th2 (IL13), Th17 (STAT3) and mast cells (TPSB2, TPSAB1).

CONCLUSION: ARNTL2 may be linked with the functional modulation of the tumour immune microenvironment and serve as a potential biomarker for predicting the prognosis of TNBC patients.

Solution Circadian Cancer Breast Clock gene Evidence Expression Full text yes yes yes no patient_samples_or_cohort yes no
  • Clock gene: no. ARNTL2 is not ARNTL. It is a paralogue (BMAL2) and is not on the core list. The "8 circadian genes" are not named, so they do not count either.
  • Full text: no. Follows from question 4. This is the abstract a keyword match on "ARNTL" lets through.
  • Evidence: patient_samples_or_cohort. Tumour transcriptomes from TCGA and GEO are patient samples, even though someone else collected them.

docs.title: Abstract 9
docs.text:
Computational Analyses Reveal Deregulated Clock Genes Associated with Breast Cancer Development in Night Shift Workers. Int J Mol Sci, 2024. PMID 39201344.

Breast cancer (BC) is the leading cause of cancer death among women worldwide. Women employed in shift jobs face heightened BC risk due to prolonged exposure to night shift work (NSW), classified as potentially carcinogenic by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). This risk is linked to disruptions in circadian rhythms governed by clock genes at the cellular level. However, the molecular mechanisms are unclear. This study aimed to assess clock genes as potential BC biomarkers among women exposed to long-term NSW. Clock gene expression was analysed in paired BC and normal breast tissues within Nurses' Health Studies I and II GEO datasets. Validation was performed on additional gene expression datasets from healthy night shift workers and women with varying BC susceptibility, as well as single-cell sequencing datasets. Post-transcriptional regulators of clock genes were identified through miRNA analyses. Significant alterations in clock gene expression in BC compared to normal tissues were found. BHLHE40, CIART, CLOCK, PDPK1, and TIMELESS were over-expressed, while HLF, NFIL3, NPAS3, PER1, PER3, SIM1, and TEF were under-expressed. The downregulation of PER1 and TEF and upregulation of CLOCK correlated with increased BC risk in healthy women. Also, twenty-six miRNAs, including miR-10a, miR-21, miR-107, and miR-34, were identified as potential post-transcriptional regulators influenced by NSW. In conclusion, a panel of clock genes and circadian miRNAs are suggested as BC susceptibility biomarkers among night shift workers, supporting implications for risk stratification and early detection strategies.

Solution Circadian Cancer Breast Clock gene Evidence Expression Full text yes yes yes yes patient_samples_or_cohort yes yes
  • Compare with abstract 3. Same cohorts, same exposure, opposite answer: here CLOCK, PER1 and PER3 are measured "in paired BC and normal breast tissues", so the clock gene is named and the evidence is tissue, not epidemiology.
  • Full text: yes. Reanalysing public data is original research.
  • Most of the other genes listed (BHLHE40, TIMELESS, NFIL3, TEF) are not core. One core gene is enough.

docs.title: Abstract 10
docs.text:
Time-of-Day of Initial Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Administration and Its Impact on Outcomes in Metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer. JCO Oncol Pract, 2026. PMID 42981555.

PURPOSE: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are integral to first-line treatment of metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Circadian biology may influence antitumor immunity, raising the hypothesis that time-of-day of ICI administration could affect outcomes. We evaluated the association between initial and cumulative ICI administration time-of-day and clinical outcomes in metastatic NSCLC.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 778 patients with metastatic NSCLC treated with first-line ICI-containing therapy across Mayo Clinic sites between January 2021 and March 2024. Patients were stratified by time-of-day of first ICI administration: early (0700-1200) versus late (1201-2400). Primary end points were overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS); the secondary end point was immune-related toxicity. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for clinically relevant covariates. Exploratory analyses evaluated cumulative infusion time-of-day and alternative administration-time thresholds using spline and cut-point analyses.

RESULTS: Of 778 patients, 277 received early and 501 received late initial ICI administration. Median OS was 1.33 versus 1.48 versus years and median PFS was 0.65 versus 0.67 years in the late and early groups, respectively. Time-of-day of initial ICI administration was not associated with OS (HR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.85 to 1.20]) or PFS (HR, 1.03 [95% CI, 0.88 to 1.21]). Findings were unchanged after multivariable adjustment. Immune-related toxicity occurred in 26.9% and 24.2% of patients in the late and early groups, respectively (P = .40). Cumulative infusion time-of-day was not associated with OS or PFS, and spline analyses identified no significant administration-time threshold associated with outcomes.

CONCLUSION: In this large real-world cohort of patients with metastatic NSCLC, neither initial nor cumulative ICI administration time-of-day was associated with survival or immune-related toxicity. Prospective studies incorporating chronotype and circadian biomarkers are warranted to further define the role of chronotherapy in immuno-oncology.

PER3 expression in granulosa cells of women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a potential role of the ovarian peripheral clock in infertility. Mol Biol Rep, 2026. PMID 41746518.

BACKGROUND: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder associated with infertility, metabolic dysfunction, and circadian rhythms disturbances, including delayed melatonin secretion. The human Period3 (PER3) plays an important role in regulating tissue-specific peripheral circadian clock. This suggests that the PER3 may be an important component of the ovarian circadian clock and could contribute to PCOS pathogenesis. METHODS AND RESULTS: At first, PCOS-related RNAseq studies retrieved from the GEO database and analyzed to find differential gene expression in PCOS datasets. In experimental step, follicular fluid and surrounding cumulus cells were collected from 16 PCOS patients and 12 healthy women. Isolated granulosa cells from follicular fluid were cultured in α-MEM supplemented with the addition of follicular fluid and harvested at 2-hour intervals over 12 h timepoints. PER3 gene expression was measured by real-time PCR. Melatonin and estrogen hormone concentrations in follicular fluid were measured using ELISA. Both RNA-seq and qPCR showed a significant increase in PER3 gene expression in PCOS patients compared to controls. Also, the normal oscillation patterns of PER3 were disrupted in PCOS patients. Melatonin and estrogen levels were significantly reduced in PCOS group. CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that increased PER3 gene expression and disruption of its rhythmicity in granulosa cells appear to be associated with PCOS. This circadian disruption may contribute to changes in melatonin and estrogen levels, potentially contributing to the development of PCOS symptoms.

Circadian Rhythm Disruption in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer: Molecular Insights and Treatment Strategies. J Pineal Res, 2025. PMID 40193174.

Disruption of the circadian clock has been closely linked to the initiation, development, and progression of cancer. This study aims to explore the impact of circadian rhythm disruption (CRD) on triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). We analyzed bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing data to assess circadian rhythm status in TNBC using multiple bioinformatic tools, alongside metabolomic profiles and tumor microenvironment evaluations to understand the influence of CRD on metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion. The results indicate that TNBC experiences profound CRD. Patients with a higher CRDscore exhibit significantly poorer relapse-free survival compared to those with a lower CRDscore. Cyclic ordering by periodic structure (CYCLOPS) identified significant changes in rhythmic gene expression patterns between TNBC and normal tissues, with TNBC showing a "rush hour" effect, where peak expression times are concentrated within specific time windows. Transcripts with disrupted circadian rhythms in TNBC were found to be involved in key pathways related to cell cycle regulation, metabolism, and immune response. Metabolomic analysis further revealed that TNBCs with high CRDscore are enriched in carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism pathways, notably showing upregulation of tryptophan metabolism. High CRDscore was also linked to an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, characterized by reduced immune cell infiltration, exhausted CD8+ T cells, and a diminished response to immune checkpoint blockade therapy. These findings suggest that the disrupted molecular clock in TNBC may activate tryptophan metabolism, thereby promoting immune evasion and potentially reducing the effectiveness of immunotherapy.
